awd_abstract_narration:
The 2025 Midwest Optimization Meeting (Recent Advances in Optimization, Control Theory, and Applications) will be the latest instance of an annual conference that began at Western Michigan University in 1997, and which for many years has provided a unique educational opportunity for graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early-career faculty.  Optimization is one of the major branches of applied mathematics, and has significant applications in different parts of science and engineering.  The 2025 Midwest Optimization Meeting will feature plenary speakers who will review the most recent advances and trends in optimization, as well as recent applications to machine/deep learning and data science.  Conference support will allow graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early-career faculty to attend, to contribute talks, and to interact with leading researchers in this vast and rapidly expanding area of study.
Thematic areas of emphasis for the 2025 Midwest Optimization Meeting include non-smooth optimization, control theory, and computational mathematics and large-scale optimization.  Applications within these areas include optimization in data science, such as over-parameterization in deep learning, distributed federated learning, control theory in deep learning, stochastic optimization, parametric optimization, and statistical optimization.  Conference plenary speakers are experts in variational and convex analysis, optimization in machine learning/data science, and optimal control.  The conference website, with registration link, travel information, and conference schedule is at https://25midwestoptimization.vfairs.com/en/, and will be updated frequently in the time leading up to the event.  The event will be open to anyone interested in the conference themes.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The University of North Dakota (UND) Department of Mathematics and Statistics hosted the 2025 Midwest Optimization Meeting (MOM 2025) on October 31–November 1, 2025. MOM is an annual research conference that brings together researchers, faculty members, postdoctoral researchers, and students working in optimization and related areas of mathematics and its applications. Each year, the meeting is hosted by a different university in the Midwest and surrounding regions.

The primary intellectual goal of MOM 2025 was to promote the exchange of recent research results and emerging ideas in optimization, convex and variational analysis, computational mathematics, and related applications. These areas provide mathematical tools for finding effective solutions to complex problems arising in areas such as control, machine learning and data analysis, logistics, and engineering design. The meeting provided opportunities for researchers to present new theoretical results, computational methods, and applications, while receiving feedback and developing new research connections.

Approximately 80 participants attended the meeting, including faculty members, postdoctoral researchers, and students from universities across the United States and abroad. The program featured four plenary speakers from Wayne State University, the University of Washington, the University of Waterloo, and Michigan State University, as well as approximately 34 contributed presentations. The contributed talks were organized into three parallel sessions: Numerical and Stochastic Optimization; Optimization Theory and Control Theory; and Optimization in Data Science, Statistics, and Applications. These sessions provided opportunities for participants to present and discuss a broad range of recent research in optimization and related mathematical fields. Contributed presenters represented a diverse group of institutions, including the University of North Dakota, North Dakota State University, South Dakota State University, the University of Minnesota, University of Rhode Island, University of Kentucky, Wayne State University, Kent State University, Loyola University Chicago, Northwest Missouri State University, North Carolina State University, Oakland University, San Diego State University, and the University of British Columbia. The detailed information of the conference can be found on the website https://25midwestoptimization.vfairs.com/en/

A significant outcome of the conference was the opportunity for students and early-career researchers to interact directly with established researchers in the field. Many students traveled from universities outside North Dakota to present their work, learn about current developments, and establish professional connections. NSF support was used to provide travel and lodging assistance to many student and early-career researcher participants, reducing financial barriers to participation. This support helped broaden access to the research community and allowed participants from institutions with limited travel resources to participate in a national research meeting.

The conference also strengthened the research environment at UND. Faculty and students from UND and neighboring institutions, including North Dakota State University and South Dakota State University, interacted with researchers from universities across the country and internationally. These interactions provided opportunities for future collaborations, research exchanges, and professional development. Hosting MOM 2025 also increased the visibility of UND's mathematics research and demonstrated the university's capacity to organize and support a regional research conference.

The meeting was organized by Bryce Christopherson, Adewale Lukman, Thanh Phat Vo, and Ryan Zerr of the UND Department of Mathematics and Statistics. Their collective efforts, together with contributions from speakers, participants, and university staff, made the conference possible.

Overall, MOM 2025 successfully advanced mathematical research in optimization by facilitating the exchange of new ideas and results, while also providing valuable training, networking, and professional development opportunities for students and early-career researchers. The meeting strengthened connections among researchers and contributed to the broader development of the optimization research community.
